claims.claim: OneLake security RLS roles don't support dynamic and multitable queries; OneLake security uses grant roles only and is deny by default.

OneLake security allows 250 roles per item (1,000 on request) and 500 members per role; role definition changes take about 5 minutes and user group changes about an hour, with some engines needing an extra hour.

Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint RLS uses CREATE SECURITY POLICY with inline table-valued function predicates; a predicate can join another table; the documented example compares a column with USER_NAME(); Direct Lake on a warehouse falls back to DirectQuery under RLS.

Entra dynamic membership group rules such as user.department -eq "Sales"; each unique member needs a Microsoft Entra ID P1 licence; Microsoft advises auditing write permissions on attributes used in rules, including those synced from on-premises Active Directory.

concept_html:
RBAC and ABAC. Role-based access control (RBAC) grants access by membership: you are in the HR analysts role, so you read the HR tables. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) decides from attributes such as department, country or business unit. Talent data needs ABAC, because the usual rule is "a manager sees their own business unit".

OneLake security is role-based. Roles only grant, and deny is the default. Its row filters are static: "RLS roles don't support dynamic and multitable queries" (Microsoft Learn, page dated 19 August 2026). A role cannot look up who is asking. Two patterns bring attributes in.

Pattern 1: attributes build the groups. A Microsoft Entra dynamic membership group adds every user whose attributes match a rule, such as user.department -eq "HR". Map each group to a OneLake security role with a static row filter for that value. Limits: each member needs a Microsoft Entra ID P1 licence, an item holds 250 roles, and a group change takes about an hour to reach OneLake.

Pattern 2: an entitlements table. In a Warehouse or the SQL analytics endpoint, CREATE SECURITY POLICY adds a filter predicate written as an inline table-valued function. The function can join an entitlements table on USER_NAME(), so one policy serves every user. It filters T-SQL queries on those items only.

Who writes the attributes? Access is only as safe as the attribute behind it. Microsoft advises you to audit who can write each attribute a dynamic group rule reads, in Entra and in on-premises Active Directory. Treat the entitlements table the same way.

Status: OneLake security RLS, Warehouse RLS and Entra dynamic groups are GA (Microsoft Learn, November 2026).

lines: CREATE FUNCTION Security.fn_unit(@unit AS varchar(50))
RETURNS TABLE
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
RETURN SELECT 1 AS allowed
FROM Security.entitlements AS e
WHERE e.upn = USER_NAME() AND e.business_unit = @unit;
GO
CREATE SECURITY POLICY Security.unit_filter
ADD FILTER PREDICATE Security.fn_unit(business_unit)
ON talent.fact_headcount
WITH (STATE = ON);

lines: CREATE FUNCTION Security.fn_unit(@unit AS varchar(50))
RETURNS TABLE
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
RETURN SELECT 1 AS allowed
WHERE (@unit = 'Retail' AND USER_NAME() = 'a.khan@example.com')
OR (@unit = 'Audit' AND USER_NAME() = 'j.lee@example.com');

exercises.primer:
`dict.get(key, default)` returns the value for `key`, or `default` when the key is missing:

```python
prices = {"tea": 2}
prices.get("tea", 0)      # 2
prices.get("coffee", 0)   # 0
```

`str.lower()` returns a lower-case copy: `"Ann@Example.com".lower()` is `"ann@example.com"`.

exercises.prompt:
Write `allowed_rows(rows: list[dict], entitlements: dict[str, list[str]], user: str) -> list[dict]`. It mirrors an entitlements predicate.

Each row has a `"business_unit"` key. `entitlements` maps a user principal name, in lower case, to the business units that user may see. Return the rows whose business unit the user may see, in their original order.

- Match `user` without regard to case, because user principal names are case-insensitive.
- A user with no entry sees no rows.
- A row with no `"business_unit"` key is never returned.
exercises.prompt_html:
Write allowed_rows(rows: list[dict], entitlements: dict[str, list[str]], user: str) -> list[dict]. It mirrors an entitlements predicate.

Each row has a "business_unit" key. entitlements maps a user principal name, in lower case, to the business units that user may see. Return the rows whose business unit the user may see, in their original order.

  • Match user without regard to case, because user principal names are case-insensitive.
  • A user with no entry sees no rows.
  • A row with no "business_unit" key is never returned.
exercises.solution:
def allowed_rows(
    rows: list[dict], entitlements: dict[str, list[str]], user: str
) -> list[dict]:
    """Rows the user may see, from an entitlements map.

    Args:
        rows: Dicts with a "business_unit" key.
        entitlements: Lower-case user principal name to allowed business units.
        user: The user principal name of the person asking.

    Returns:
        The allowed rows in their original order. Empty for a user with no entry.
    """
    units = set(entitlements.get(user.lower(), []))
    return [row for row in rows if row.get("business_unit") in units]

title: Attribute-based access, rows by business unit
why_html: A talent team built one OneLake role per manager, with the manager's name in each row filter. After a reorganisation, 40 roles needed edits by hand, and 6 were missed for two weeks. Managers who had moved still saw their old teams' salaries. An entitlements table that HR maintains, read by one policy, would have needed one data change per move.
